evals.prompt: I'm the platform lead at Parcelforge, a logistics API used by about 900 integrators. We're finally building a proper status page. My plan: list all 38 of our microservices as components so customers see exactly what's affected, use our own lifecycle vocabulary (Detected, Diagnosing, Patching, Stable) because it matches our internal runbooks, and use a six-color severity scale so we can express nuance. Also, last month our Frankfurt data center went fully down for 40 minutes while everything else was fine, and we argued about how to represent that. Design the component and status model for us.
evals.expected_output: A status-page model that rejects the microservice mirror and custom vocabulary, uses the four industry lifecycle statuses and four visual states, defines severity by breadth of impact, aggregates top-level status from the worst component with a documented blend rule, and scopes the Frankfurt case as a regional partial outage.
expectations: Rejects listing all 38 microservices as status-page components
Recommends grouping into a handful of consumer-recognizable components chosen by the user's mental model of the product (e.g. API, dashboard, webhooks, docs), not internal architecture
Rejects the custom Detected/Diagnosing/Patching/Stable lifecycle vocabulary
Uses exactly the four statuses Investigating, Identified, Monitoring, Resolved
Justifies the standard vocabulary by subscriber comprehension: readers already know the industry-wide set, a custom set costs comprehension and buys nothing
Rejects the six-color scale and caps the page at four visual states (operational / degraded / partial / major)
Defines Degraded Performance as working but slow for everyone
Defines Partial Outage as completely broken for a subset of users
Defines Major Outage as unavailable for everyone
States explicitly that component severity encodes breadth of impact, not felt severity
States that the top-level page status aggregates from the worst component state
Recommends writing the aggregation/blend rule down so it is applied consistently rather than re-argued per incident
Classifies the Frankfurt case as a Partial Outage scoped to that region, not a blanket page-wide state alarming users elsewhere

evals.prompt: We run Quotable, a pricing-data API. Our incident process: monitoring pages the on-call engineer, the engineer confirms the problem is real, then our support lead reviews the wording before anything goes on the status page - we added that step to avoid false alarms and embarrassing typos. During our last outage the page showed all green for 45 minutes of a 60-minute incident, and customers found out from a Reddit thread before we posted. Our monitoring itself is solid: health checks, latency thresholds, uptime probes on every endpoint. Tighten this process so it doesn't happen again.
evals.expected_output: A redesign that removes the human approval gate, auto-opens Investigating incidents from monitoring alerts with humans enriching afterwards, writes a staged escalation pipeline, adds a workflow-level probe, and installs detection-to-disclosure and third-party-first measurements.
expectations: Removes the human confirmation/approval gate as a precondition for the first public status change
Recommends auto-opening an Investigating incident directly from the monitoring alert
Frames the human role as enrichment (adding substance, scope, cadence) after disclosure, never as first disclosure
Rejects or re-scopes the support-lead wording review so it cannot delay the initial public post

Recommends writing down a staged escalation pipeline: an explicit rule for when an internal event becomes a public communication (alerts, incidents of note, triage, problems, status updates, published report)
Recommends adding at least one workflow-level probe exercising a real multi-step user journey, not only infrastructure checks
Distinguishes infrastructure-green from product-broken as different claims when justifying the workflow probe
Installs detection-to-disclosure lag (alert-fired to page-updated) as a per-incident measurement driven to minutes
States that a lag in the tens of minutes indicates a human gate is still in the loop
Installs zero third-party-first disclosures (no aggregator or social post beating the page) as a binary per-incident gate
Identifies customer migration to third-party complaint aggregators as the failure signal of lost trust in the page
Recommends calibrated accuracy rather than maximal alarm, noting an honestly earned green history is itself valuable

evals.prompt: Hatchbill is a self-serve invoicing API - credit-card signups only, no enterprise contracts, no SLAs with penalties anywhere. Our integrators are developers, and most already consume our product webhooks. The status page we spun up last quarter runs in the same AWS account and behind the same Route53 zone as the product itself. I have two engineers and roughly two weeks to get incident notifications right. Which notification channels should we build, and in what order? I was thinking email, SMS, maybe push later.
evals.expected_output: A ranked channel plan: page plus email/RSS as the default rung, webhook push promoted for the developer audience, SMS removed from the menu entirely with a named re-promotion trigger, and out-of-band redundancy promoted because the page shares infrastructure with the platform.
expectations: Recommends the status page with email and RSS subscription enabled as the default first rung
Notes hosted status tooling provides email/RSS subscription nearly free
States that subscriptions reduce inbound support tickets during incidents (a support-load lever, not a courtesy)
Promotes webhook push because the audience is integrating developers who wire status into their own alerting
Notes webhook push is cheap here specifically because the platform already runs webhook delivery infrastructure
Removes SMS/phone-grade push from the plan entirely rather than ranking it last or deferring it to later
Justifies the SMS deletion by the absence of contractual SLAs and enterprise customers, given its per-message cost and deliverability work
Names the SMS re-promotion trigger: the first contract that specifies a notification channel
Flags the shared AWS account / shared DNS hosting as a problem: the page dies with the platform at the only moment it matters
Promotes out-of-band redundancy (page hosted off the platform's own infrastructure, or at least one channel surviving a platform DNS/CDN failure) because of the shared hosting
Distinguishes pull (the page the customer must visit) from push (subscriptions) and states a mature practice needs both
States the channel ranking explicitly rather than leaving it implied by list order
Ties the final ordering to the user's stated answers (no contracts, developer audience, shared infra, two-week ceiling), saying which constraint moved which rung

evals.prompt: Live incident at Corklane right now - API requests have been failing for 20 minutes. My draft for the status page, internally we're tracking it as INC-CORK-77 'Operation Redwing': "Operation Redwing - We believe this is an upstream AWS networking problem. Our k8s ingress pods keep getting rescheduled by the operator, which churns the endpoints. Will post more when we know more." Can you clean this up and post-ready it? We haven't actually confirmed the AWS theory yet, but it's our best guess. We know retries usually succeed right now.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten update that drops the vendor blame and internal jargon, states only confirmed facts while admitting the cause is unconfirmed, carries a zoned timestamp, a plain-language title, the retry workaround, and a specific next-update time.
expectations: Removes the attribution of the incident to AWS from the public update
States the rule: never deflect to an upstream vendor in public updates, even when the root cause genuinely is upstream
Removes the internal jargon (k8s ingress pods, operator, endpoint churn) from the customer-facing text
Removes the unconfirmed AWS theory as stated fact, keeping only what is confirmed
Has the update explicitly admit the cause is not yet confirmed rather than omitting the topic
Replaces the open-ended 'will post more when we know more' with a specific next-update time
Adds a timestamp with an explicit time zone to the update
Includes the retry workaround in the update since retries are known to succeed
Replaces the 'Operation Redwing' codename with a plain-language title stating the nature of the problem
States that internal incident identifiers and codenames never surface publicly
Describes impact in the consumers' terms (what they are experiencing), not in infrastructure terms
Recommends posting now rather than waiting for a fuller picture, and keeping page, social, and email consistent with this same content

evals.prompt: Vaultic's authentication API is completely down in ap-southeast - 100% of requests failing there for the last half hour. That region is about 15% of our customer base. Our CEO wants the whole page flipped to Major Outage red because 'for those customers it IS major - total failure'. Internally we've classed it SEV2. The on-call engineer just messaged that error rates dropped back to normal two minutes ago and wants to mark the incident Resolved immediately so the outage window looks shorter. What do we set on the page and what do we post?
evals.expected_output: Classification as a regionally-scoped Partial Outage per the breadth axis and the written SEV mapping, a Monitoring stage before Resolved instead of instant closure, and a Resolved update that quantifies the window and scope, owns the impact, and commits to a follow-up summary.
expectations: Sets the component to Partial Outage, not Major Outage, despite the CEO's framing
Justifies via the breadth axis: completely broken for a subset (one region) is the definition of Partial Outage; Major Outage means unavailable for everyone
Scopes the incident to ap-southeast in the title or scope statement so users elsewhere are not alarmed
Rejects marking the incident Resolved immediately upon error rates recovering
Moves the incident to Monitoring status with the recovery noted and the incident held open under observation
Explains that resolving on the first green minute and then reopening costs more trust than a visible monitoring period
Maps SEV2 to Partial Outage consistent with a severity-to-component-state mapping
Recommends the severity-to-public-state mapping be agreed once in writing, not debated mid-incident
Keeps the internal SEV2 label off the public page (internal severity vocabulary never surfaces publicly)
Has the eventual Resolved update quantify the impact window and affected scope (times and the affected share/region)
Has the Resolved update acknowledge or apologize for the disruption
Has the Resolved update commit to a posted summary of cause and prevention within a stated timeframe

evals.prompt: Brightmesh (data-sync API for B2B SaaS) had a 3-hour total outage last Tuesday - our worst ever, internally a P1. Enterprise customers are furious and two have mentioned churn on calls. The internal postmortem is done: it names Priya, the staff engineer whose config push triggered it, walks through our internal service mesh topology, and mentions the auth token exposure we found and fixed along the way. Legal wants us to post a one-line 'resolved, we've fixed it' note and move on. Our CTO asked me what we should actually publish, and where. We do have an active engineering blog.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to publish a full public postmortem on the engineering blog, with the argument for publishing over legal's default, a filtered and blameless external document structured around the three customer questions, split action items with owners and follow-through tracking, and acknowledgment of the sign-off and irreversibility costs.
expectations: Recommends a full public postmortem rather than the one-line resolved note
Recommends the engineering blog as the channel, since the developer audience reads the deep version for trust-building
Justifies promotion by the P1/major class of the incident and the visibly shaken trust
Counters legal's default with the SRE argument: sharing a postmortem widely multiplies its learning value, and an honest postmortem is a key tool in restoring shaken trust
Removes Priya's name from the public document, referring to a role instead of a person
States the blameless rule concretely: never name an individual human in the published document
Applies an explicit internal-to-external filtering step rather than publishing the internal document as-is
Filters out the internal service-mesh/topology detail beyond what the explanation needs
Filters out the security-sensitive auth-token detail
Structures the external document around: why did this happen; could it have been worse; how do we make sure it won't happen again
Includes a 'could it have been worse / where we got lucky' section transferred close to as-is from the internal version
Includes a UTC timeline from first alert to resolution and quantified impact figures
Splits action items into mitigative and preventative, each with an owner and a status
Commits to publicly updating action-item status, noting completion below roughly 50% is the threshold at which postmortems become theater
Warns that publication is irreversible (a correction can be appended, an admission cannot be unpublished) and that the deep write-up triggers legal/comms sign-off on cause language

evals.prompt: Meterly sells a usage-metering API. Marketing wants a big '99.99% uptime' banner and a public uptime page to close enterprise deals. Reality: our internal reliability target is 99.9%, our contracts today promise nothing specific, and we've never written down what counts as 'down' - last quarter we had two separate 20-minute periods where p50 latency doubled but requests still succeeded, and we counted both as 100% up. Build the public uptime page for us.
evals.expected_output: A public reporting design that keeps SLI/SLO/SLA distinct, refuses to publish the aspirational 99.99%, defines the downtime edge cases in writing first, translates percentages into minutes, publishes incident history beside the headline figure with the degraded-counts-as-up caveat surfaced, and separates the SLA page from the status page.
expectations: Distinguishes SLIs (measured metrics), SLOs (internal targets), and SLAs (contractual commitments with consequences) in the design
Refuses to publish 99.99% while the internal target is 99.9%, identifying an aspirational number presented as a commitment as a dispute source
Requires the edge cases be defined in writing before any number is published
Defines a response-time threshold above which a slow response counts as downtime
Defines whether the number is evaluated service-wide or per affected component, consistent with the status page's breadth model
States planned maintenance is excluded from the arithmetic only when adequate notice was given, with that condition written into the SLA text
Flags monitoring calibration: probing too sensitively overcounts downtime, too coarsely undercounts it, either corrupting the published number
Translates the percentage target into allowed downtime minutes published alongside it (e.g. 99.9% as roughly 43 minutes per month, 99.99% as roughly 4.3 minutes per month)
Publishes incident history next to the headline uptime figure
Explains that Degraded Performance conventionally counts as 0% downtime, which is exactly how the two latency-doubling periods vanished from the number
Recommends the latency-doubling periods surface as incidents (degraded state) rather than remaining invisible behind a 100% figure
Treats the SLA/uptime page and the status page as distinct artifacts: historical performance against commitments versus current discrete incidents
Recommends offering both pages, cross-linked

evals.prompt: Draftify (document-generation API) is migrating its primary database in 12 days: about two hours where document-write calls will fail, reads unaffected. Ops picked Saturday 8pm US-Eastern 'because the office is closed then' - though most of our customers run batch jobs from Asia-Pacific overnight. We have one enterprise contract that requires 5 business days notice for planned downtime. Marketing wants to bundle into the same announcement that our legacy v1 endpoints are being retired at the end of next year, 'since we're emailing everyone anyway'. Current draft: 'Heads up - the API will be down for a couple hours Saturday night for maintenance.' Plan the communication.
evals.expected_output: A maintenance-communication plan that separates the v1 retirement into its own communication track, rewrites the notice with exact zoned times and precise affected/unaffected scope plus expected behavior, honors the contractual notice floor, reschedules against customers' low-traffic hours, delivers via page plus push with reminders and start/completion confirmations.
expectations: Removes the v1 endpoint retirement from the maintenance announcement, making it a separate communication

Justifies the split: a maintenance window and a deprecation are different communications on different timelines (day-to-week notice versus a multi-month runway) and must never be blended into one announcement
Rewrites the notice with exact start and end times
States an explicit time zone for those times
States precise scope: write/document-generation calls affected, reads and other surfaces unaffected - replacing the blanket 'the API will be down'
States what consumers should expect and do during the window (e.g. failing write calls, whether to pause batch jobs or retry)
Verifies the schedule satisfies the enterprise contract's 5-business-day notice floor
Challenges the Saturday-8pm-Eastern choice: schedule against the affected users' low-traffic hours, not the provider's office hours, given the Asia-Pacific overnight batch load
Delivers the notice via the status page plus at least one push channel, never the page alone
Schedules a reminder notification as the date approaches, in addition to the initial notice
Posts start and completion confirmations even for the short two-hour window
Notes that SLA exclusion is not trust exclusion: a badly communicated window still costs trust even when the arithmetic forgives it
